meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Suppose scores on an easy exam have a mean of 72 and a median of 84. What does this suggest about the distribution of scores?

options.text: It is left-skewed: a few very low scores pull the mean below the median.
options.feedback: Correct. When a long tail of low values pulls the mean down, the mean sits below the median: the signature of left skewness.

options.text: It is right-skewed: the mean is below the median, so the tail points right.
options.feedback: The direction is reversed. A mean below the median means the extreme values are on the low side, so the long tail points to the left.

options.text: It is symmetric: the mean and the median are both measures of the center.
options.feedback: In a symmetric distribution the mean and median are close. A 12-point gap signals asymmetry.

options.text: Most students scored below the mean of 72.
options.feedback: With a median of 84, at least half of the students scored 84 or more, well above the mean.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.1: the mean is sensitive to extreme values, the median is not. A mean well below the median means a few very low scores stretch the left tail, so the distribution is left-skewed.

practice.stem: For the sample {5, 2, 2, 8, 3}, what is the median?

options.feedback: Correct. Sorted, the data are 2, 2, 3, 5, 8, and the middle (third) value is 3.
2 is the most frequent value (the mode). The median is the middle value of the sorted data.
8 is the largest value. Sort the data first and take the value in the middle position.
4 is the mean: (5 + 2 + 2 + 8 + 3) ÷ 5. The median is the middle value of the sorted data.

practice.explanation: The median is the middle value once the data are sorted: 2, 2, 3, 5, 8 gives 3. The mean is 4, pulled up slightly by the 8.

practice.stem: Adding one extremely large value to a dataset changes the mean more than the median.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The mean includes the size of every value, so one huge value drags it up; the median moves at most to a neighboring observation.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Think about how each statistic uses the new value: the mean uses its size, while the median uses only its position in the sorted list.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.1: the median is more robust to outliers than the mean. That is why the median is preferred for skewed data such as earnings and wealth.

practice.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: A box plot shows a lower quartile (Q1) of 25, a median of 35, and an upper quartile (Q3) of 70. What is the interquartile range (IQR)?

options.feedback: 10 is the distance from Q1 to the median, which covers only a quarter of the data.
Correct. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 70 − 25 = 45, the width of the middle half of the data.
35 is the median (and also the distance from the median to Q3). The IQR is the distance between the two quartiles.
The IQR is a distance between two quartiles, so it comes from a difference, not a sum.

practice.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 70 − 25 = 45. Here the median (35) sits much closer to Q1 than to Q3, a hint of right skewness in the middle of the data.

practice.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: Suppose commute times in a city have a mean of 30 minutes and a standard deviation of 8 minutes. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: About 8% of workers commute longer than 30 minutes.
options.feedback: The standard deviation is measured in minutes, not as a percentage of people.

options.text: Every worker's commute lasts between 22 and 38 minutes.
options.feedback: The standard deviation is a typical distance from the mean, not a hard limit; some commutes are longer or shorter.

options.text: Commute times typically differ from the mean by roughly 8 minutes.
options.feedback: Correct. The standard deviation measures the typical distance of observations from the mean.

options.text: Half of the workers commute between 8 and 30 minutes.
options.feedback: This treats the standard deviation as if it were a quartile. Quartiles, not the standard deviation, split the data into halves and quarters.

practice.explanation: The standard deviation measures how far observations typically are from the mean: commutes typically differ from 30 minutes by about 8 minutes. It is not a bound, and it does not split the data into shares.

practice.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: A variable is approximately normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: About 50% of observations fall between 40 and 60.
options.feedback: The band from 40 to 60 is one standard deviation on each side of the mean. For bell-shaped data that band holds more than half of the observations.

options.text: About 68% of observations fall between 40 and 60.
options.feedback: Correct: about 68% of bell-shaped data lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

options.text: About 95% of observations fall between 30 and 70.
options.feedback: Correct: about 95% of bell-shaped data lie within two standard deviations of the mean.

options.text: Almost no observations fall between 30 and 40.
options.feedback: Roughly 13–14% of observations lie between one and two standard deviations below the mean, which is far from none.

practice.explanation: For approximately normal data, about 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean (40 to 60 here) and about 95% within two (30 to 70). This is a rule of thumb for bell-shaped data only.

practice.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: A dataset has a skewness of −0.85. Using the chapter's guideline, how is the distribution best described?

options.text: Highly right-skewed, with a long tail of high values
options.feedback: A negative skewness points the long tail toward low values, and 0.85 in absolute value is below the 'highly skewed' cutoff.

options.text: Approximately symmetric, because the value is below 1
options.feedback: The guideline treats values between 0.5 and 1 in absolute value as moderate skewness, not symmetry.

options.text: Moderately right-skewed, because the value is below 1
options.feedback: The size of the number sets the strength, but its sign sets the direction. Check the sign.

options.text: Moderately left-skewed, with the mean likely below the median
options.feedback: Correct. |−0.85| is between 0.5 and 1 (moderate), and the negative sign means a longer tail of low values, which pulls the mean below the median.

practice.explanation: Skewness guideline: |skewness| < 0.5 approximately symmetric, 0.5–1 moderately skewed, above 1 highly skewed. The sign gives the direction: negative means a longer left tail, which usually puts the mean below the median.

practice.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: Distribution X has an excess kurtosis of −0.8; distribution Y has an excess kurtosis of +3.0. Which one tends to produce extreme values more often?

options.text: Neither: kurtosis only tells you whether the distribution is skewed
options.feedback: Asymmetry is measured by skewness. Kurtosis is a separate shape measure.

options.text: X, because negative excess kurtosis signals more outliers
options.feedback: Negative excess kurtosis means lighter tails than the normal distribution, so extreme values are less common.

options.text: Neither: kurtosis measures the center of a distribution, not its tails
options.feedback: Kurtosis is a shape measure about tail heaviness; the center is described by the mean and median.

options.text: Y, because positive excess kurtosis means heavier tails than a normal distribution
options.feedback: Correct. Excess kurtosis above 0 means fatter tails, so extreme values appear more often than a bell curve would predict.

practice.explanation: Excess kurtosis compares tail heaviness with the normal distribution (excess kurtosis 0): above 0 means heavier tails and more frequent extremes; below 0 means lighter tails.

practice.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
practice.stem: An excess kurtosis of 0 means the tails are heavier than those of a normal distribution.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how excess kurtosis is defined: it is measured relative to a benchmark distribution. Which one?

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. An excess kurtosis of 0 means tails as heavy as the normal distribution's; heavier tails show up as positive values.

practice.explanation: Excess kurtosis = raw kurtosis − 3, and the normal distribution has raw kurtosis 3, so its excess kurtosis is 0. Positive values mean heavier tails; negative values mean lighter tails.

practice.stem: In a box plot, the median line sits in the middle of the box and the two whiskers have about the same length. What does this suggest?

options.text: The distribution is right-skewed.
options.feedback: Right skewness would show up as a median closer to the lower edge of the box and a longer upper whisker.

options.text: The distribution is left-skewed.
options.feedback: Left skewness would mean a long tail of low values, so the plot would be lopsided rather than balanced.

options.text: The distribution is roughly symmetric.
options.feedback: Correct. A centered median and balanced whiskers indicate a roughly symmetric distribution.

options.text: The data contain no observations outside the box.
options.feedback: The whiskers themselves represent observations outside the box; equal whiskers say nothing about whether data lie beyond the quartiles.

practice.explanation: In a box plot, the position of the median inside the box and the relative whisker lengths reveal asymmetry. Centered median plus balanced whiskers means roughly symmetric.

practice.stem: Which features does a standard box plot display? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The median
options.feedback: Correct: the line inside the box marks the median.

options.text: The standard deviation
options.feedback: A box plot is built from quartiles, not from the standard deviation.

options.text: The first and third quartiles (the edges of the box)
options.feedback: Correct: the box runs from Q1 to Q3, the interquartile range.

options.text: Outliers beyond the whiskers
options.feedback: Correct: points beyond the whiskers are drawn individually as outliers.

practice.explanation: A box plot shows the median, the quartiles (the box covers the IQR), whiskers to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the quartiles, and individual dots for outliers beyond them.

practice.concept: Histograms and kernel density estimates (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2)
practice.stem: A histogram drawn with very narrow bins looks jagged, with many small peaks. What is the most sensible next step?

options.text: Conclude that the data contain many distinct groups.
options.feedback: Narrow bins add noise: small peaks may just reflect where a few observations happen to fall.

options.text: Try several bin widths, including wider ones, before drawing conclusions.
options.feedback: Correct. Comparing bin widths separates the overall shape from noise.

options.text: Discard the histogram, since histograms cannot show distributions.
options.feedback: Histograms are a standard way to show distributions; the issue here is only the choice of bin width.

options.text: Switch to a pie chart, which handles numerical data better.
options.feedback: Pie charts show shares of categories, not the distribution of a numerical variable.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.2: bin width is a choice, and small peaks in a narrow-bin histogram may just reflect where a few observations happen to fall. Compare several widths before drawing conclusions.

practice.concept: Histograms and kernel density estimates (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2)
practice.stem: The vertical axis of a kernel density estimate shows how many observations take each value.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what the vertical axis of a kernel density estimate measures (Section 2.2).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A kernel density estimate is a smooth curve whose vertical axis shows density, not counts of observations.

practice.explanation: A kernel density estimate is a smoothed estimate of the probability density; its vertical axis shows density rather than frequency counts (Section 2.2).

practice.stem: For monthly temperature readings over one year, a line chart reveals the seasonal pattern better than a histogram does.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A line chart keeps the time order and shows the seasonal cycle; a histogram shows only how often each temperature range occurs.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Ask whether the readings have a natural order in time, and which chart keeps that order.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.3: line charts suit time-ordered data, revealing trends and seasonal cycles. Histograms show the distribution of values and ignore when each value occurred.

practice.concept: Charts for numerical data by category (Section 2.3, Key Concept 2.4)
practice.stem: A city wants to chart its budget across 10 departments in a bar chart. Why sort the bars from largest to smallest?

options.text: So the ranking of departments can be read at a glance.
options.feedback: Correct. Sorting makes the comparison across categories immediate, which is the purpose of a bar chart.

options.text: Because a bar chart is invalid unless the bars are sorted.
options.feedback: Unsorted bar charts are still valid; sorting is a design choice that makes comparisons easier.

options.text: So that the bars add up to 100% of the budget.
options.feedback: Sorting changes only the order of the bars, not their heights or their total.

options.text: Because sorting removes the smallest departments from the chart.
options.feedback: Sorting keeps every category; it only changes the order.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.4: bar charts use bar length to represent values, so comparisons across categories are immediate. Sorting by size makes the ranking instantly readable.

practice.concept: Charts for numerical data by category (Section 2.3, Key Concept 2.4)
practice.stem: Suppose a city spends $40 million on schools, $25 million on roads, $15 million on parks, and $20 million on other items. What share of the total goes to roads?

options.text: About 40%
options.feedback: That is the share of schools, the largest category.

options.text: About 62.5%
options.feedback: This compares roads with schools (25 ÷ 40). A share compares a category with the total of all categories.

options.text: About 20%
options.feedback: That is the share of other items. Divide the roads figure by the total.

options.text: About 25%
options.feedback: Correct: the total is $100 million, so roads take 25 ÷ 100 = 25%.

practice.explanation: A category's share = category value ÷ total of all categories. Here the total is 40 + 25 + 15 + 20 = $100 million, so roads take 25%.

practice.concept: Charts for categorical data (Section 2.4, Key Concept 2.5)
practice.stem: Suppose that in a survey of 200 commuters, 90 drive, 60 take public transit, 30 walk, and 20 cycle. What is the relative frequency of public transit?

options.feedback: 60 is the frequency (count). The relative frequency divides the count by the total number of commuters.
Correct: 60 ÷ 200 = 0.30, or 30% of commuters.
This divides by the number of non-drivers (150). Relative frequency uses all 200 commuters.
60 ÷ 200 = 0.30 as a proportion; check the conversion to a percentage.

practice.explanation: Relative frequency = count ÷ total. 60 ÷ 200 = 0.30, so 30% of commuters take public transit. A frequency table lists both counts and relative frequencies.

practice.concept: Charts for categorical data (Section 2.4, Key Concept 2.5)
practice.stem: Which of these variables are categorical, so that a frequency table is the natural summary? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Brand of smartphone owned
options.feedback: Correct: each person falls into one brand category.

options.text: Monthly rent in dollars
options.feedback: Rent is numerical and can take many values; summary statistics and histograms suit it better.

options.text: Annual household income in dollars
options.feedback: Income is numerical; it is summarized with statistics such as the mean, median, and standard deviation.

options.text: Region of residence (North, South, East, West)
options.feedback: Correct: the values are labels for groups.

practice.explanation: Categorical variables record which group an observation belongs to (a label); numerical variables record a measured quantity that can take many values.

practice.stem: Which variable is most likely to become more symmetric after a natural log transformation?

options.text: Monthly temperature anomalies, which are symmetric around zero
options.feedback: These values include zero and negatives, where the log is undefined, and the data are already symmetric.

options.text: Scores on an easy test where most students are near the maximum
options.feedback: The log stretches out small values, which would make a long left tail even longer.

options.text: City populations, which are all positive with a few very large cities
options.feedback: Correct. Strictly positive, right-skewed data are exactly where the log compresses the long right tail.

options.text: Region of residence (North, South, East, West)
options.feedback: Region is categorical; a logarithm needs positive numerical values.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.6: natural logs convert right-skewed, strictly positive data (populations, prices, earnings, wealth) into more symmetric distributions. Logs are undefined for zero or negative values.

practice.stem: Suppose log earnings rise by 0.5. The small-change approximation suggests about a 50% increase in earnings. What is the exact increase, \( 100\,(e^{0.5}-1) \)?

options.text: About 65%
options.feedback: Correct: \( e^{0.5} \approx 1.65 \), so earnings rise by about 65%. The 50% approximation is only accurate for small changes.

options.text: Exactly 50%
options.feedback: The approximation 'change in log ≈ proportional change' works for small changes; 0.5 is large enough for it to be noticeably off.

options.text: About 0.5%
options.feedback: A change of 0.5 in log points is large; compute \( e^{0.5} \) to see the multiplicative change.

options.text: About 165%
options.feedback: \( e^{0.5} \approx 1.65 \) is the ratio of new to old earnings; the percentage increase subtracts 1 from that ratio.

practice.explanation: A change of Δ in log earnings multiplies earnings by \( e^{\Delta} \). For Δ = 0.5, \( e^{0.5} \approx 1.649 \), an increase of about 65%. The rule 'Δln(x) ≈ proportional change' is accurate only for small changes such as 0.05.

practice.stem: An increase of 0.05 in log income corresponds to an increase in income of approximately 5%.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. For small changes, the change in the natural log approximates the proportionate change: 0.05 ≈ 5%.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the property Δln(x) ≈ Δx/x for small changes (Key Takeaways).

practice.explanation: For small changes, Δln(x) ≈ Δx/x, so an increase of 0.05 in log income is approximately a 5% increase (exactly \( e^{0.05}-1 \approx 5.1\% \)).

practice.stem: A sample has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. What is the z-score of an observation equal to 130?

options.feedback: 30 is the distance from the mean in original units. A z-score expresses that distance in standard deviations.
This divides the observation itself by the standard deviation. A z-score starts from the distance to the mean.
Correct: z = (130 − 100) ÷ 15 = 2.0, so the observation lies two standard deviations above the mean.
This divides the observation by the mean. A z-score divides the distance from the mean by the standard deviation.

practice.explanation: \( z = (x - \bar{x})/s = (130 - 100)/15 = 2 \): the observation is two standard deviations above the mean, which is unusual (|z| > 2).

practice.stem: After a variable is standardized into z-scores, what are its mean and standard deviation?

options.text: Mean 1 and standard deviation 0
options.feedback: The roles are swapped: subtracting the mean centers the data, and dividing by the standard deviation rescales the spread.

options.text: Mean 0 and standard deviation 1
options.feedback: Correct. Subtracting the mean centers the data at 0; dividing by the standard deviation makes the spread 1.

options.text: Mean 0 and the original standard deviation
options.feedback: Dividing by the standard deviation also rescales the spread.

options.text: The original mean and standard deviation
options.feedback: Standardizing changes both the center and the scale of the data.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.6: subtracting the mean centers the z-scores at 0, and dividing by the standard deviation rescales their standard deviation to 1.

practice.stem: What is the main purpose of an 11-month moving average of monthly home sales?

options.text: To convert home sales into real, inflation-adjusted values
options.feedback: Adjusting for inflation uses a price index. A moving average is about smoothing over time.

options.text: To forecast next month's home sales exactly
options.feedback: A moving average summarizes past and surrounding months; it is not an exact forecast.

options.text: To remove the long-run trend from the series
options.feedback: A moving average keeps the trend and makes it easier to see.

options.text: To smooth month-to-month swings so the underlying trend is visible
options.feedback: Correct. Averaging over 11 months smooths short-term fluctuations, revealing the trend and cycles.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 2.7: moving averages smooth short-term fluctuations by averaging over several periods. The trade-off is smoothness versus a delayed signal.

practice.stem: Suppose a city reports its total monthly retail sales in dollars from 2000 to 2020. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Seasonal adjustment and a moving average are the same transformation.
options.feedback: Seasonal adjustment removes recurring within-year patterns; a moving average smooths fluctuations by averaging neighboring periods.

options.text: Dividing sales by a price index expresses them in real (constant-dollar) terms.
options.feedback: Correct: real values remove the effect of price changes.

options.text: Real sales are always larger than nominal sales.
options.feedback: Real and nominal values coincide in the base year of the price index; which one is larger depends on whether prices were lower or higher than in the base year.

options.text: Dividing sales by the city's population gives sales per capita.
options.feedback: Correct: per capita values adjust for population size.

practice.explanation: Real values adjust for inflation using a price index; per capita values adjust for population size. Moving averages and seasonal adjustment are separate tools for time-ordered data.

exam.stem: For the 171 full-time working women aged 30, mean annual earnings are $41,413 and median earnings are $36,000. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Most of the women earn more than $41,413.
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 2.1 on how the mean and median relate in skewed data.

options.text: The distribution is roughly symmetric, because the mean and median differ by only 15%.
options.feedback: Revisit what the chapter concludes from this gap between the mean and the median (Section 2.1).

options.text: A few very high earners pull the mean up, so the distribution is right-skewed.
options.feedback: Correct. A mean above the median is the signature of a long right tail of high values.

options.text: The distribution is left-skewed, because the median is below the mean.
options.feedback: Revisit how the relative position of the mean and the median relates to the direction of the long tail (Section 2.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.1: the mean is sensitive to extreme values, the median is not. Mean $41,413 > median $36,000 because a few high earners (up to $172,000) stretch the right tail: the distribution is right-skewed.

exam.stem: The median of the 171 women's earnings is $36,000. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The mean earnings of the 171 women are $36,000.
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between the two measures of the center described in Key Concept 2.1.

options.text: Half of the women earn exactly $36,000.
options.feedback: The median is a position in the sorted data, not the value that half of the observations share.

options.text: At least half of the women earn $36,000 or less.
options.feedback: Correct. The median is the middle value of the sorted data, so at least half of the observations are at or below it.

options.text: No woman in the sample earns less than $36,000.
options.feedback: Revisit how the median splits the sorted data (Section 2.1).

exam.explanation: The median is the middle value once the data are sorted: with 171 women it is the 86th value, so at least 86 women earn $36,000 or less. In this sample, 89 women do.

exam.stem: If the highest earning in the sample ($172,000) were replaced by $500,000, the median of the 171 earnings would rise.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how the median is determined: does it depend on the size of the largest value, or only on the order of the values?

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The largest value stays the largest, so the middle value of the sorted data is unchanged; only the mean would rise.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.1: the median depends only on the order of the observations, so making the largest value even larger leaves it at $36,000. The mean, which uses every value's size, would rise by (500,000 − 172,000) ÷ 171 ≈ $1,918.

exam.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: For the 171 women, the first quartile of earnings is $25,000 and the third quartile is $49,000. Which statement about the interquartile range (IQR) is correct?

options.text: The IQR is $12,000, and it measures the spread of the middle half of the earnings.
options.feedback: Check both the value and the interpretation in this statement against the definition of the IQR (Key Concepts: Quartiles and IQR).

options.text: The IQR is $24,000, and it shows that a typical woman earns about $24,000.
options.feedback: Check both the value and the interpretation in this statement against the definition of the IQR (Key Concepts: Quartiles and IQR).

options.text: The IQR is $12,000, and it shows that a typical woman earns about $12,000.
options.feedback: Check both the value and the interpretation in this statement against the definition of the IQR (Key Concepts: Quartiles and IQR).

options.text: The IQR is $24,000, and it measures the spread of the middle half of the earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 49,000 − 25,000 = $24,000, the width of the band holding the middle 50% of the data.

exam.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = $49,000 − $25,000 = $24,000. The middle half of the women earn between $25,000 and $49,000; this is the box in the chapter's box plot.

exam.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: Suppose a sample of 30-year-old men has the same mean earnings as the 171 women ($41,413) but a standard deviation of $40,000 instead of $25,527. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Men earn more than women on average, because their standard deviation is larger.
options.feedback: Compare the two groups' means given in the question, and revisit what the standard deviation measures (Section 2.1).

options.text: Men's earnings are more spread out around the mean than women's earnings.
options.feedback: Correct. A larger standard deviation means observations typically sit further from the mean.

options.text: The two groups have the same distribution of earnings, because their means are equal.
options.feedback: Revisit whether two samples with equal means can still differ in other ways (Section 2.1).

options.text: Every man in the sample earns within $40,000 of the mean.
options.feedback: Compare with the women's data: their earnings range from $1,050 to $172,000, far more than $25,527 from the mean in places (Section 2.1).

exam.explanation: The standard deviation, \( s = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2} \), measures the typical distance from the mean. With equal means, the group with the larger standard deviation ($40,000 versus $25,527) has earnings more spread out around that mean.

exam.concept: Measures of spread: standard deviation and quartiles (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: For bell-shaped data, about 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean. In the earnings data, the band from $15,886 to $66,940 (mean ± 1 SD) actually contains about 75% of the women. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The 68% figure describes bell-shaped data, so it need not hold for every dataset.
options.feedback: Correct: the 68% (and 95%) figures describe approximately normal data.

options.text: Earnings are right-skewed rather than bell-shaped, which helps explain the gap.
options.feedback: Correct: earnings are not bell-shaped, so the bell-curve shares need not hold.

options.text: A share of 75% suggests that the standard deviation was probably miscalculated.
options.feedback: Nothing in the reported figures points to a calculation error. Revisit Section 2.1.

options.text: Because earnings are not bell-shaped, the standard deviation no longer measures their spread.
options.feedback: Revisit what the standard deviation measures, whatever the shape of the distribution (Section 2.1).

options.text: For normal data, about 95% of observations lie within two standard deviations of the mean.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the second part of the rule of thumb for bell-shaped data.

exam.explanation: The 68%–95% shares hold for approximately normal data. Earnings are right-skewed with heavy tails, so the band mean ± 1 SD ($15,886 to $66,940) holds about 75% of the women instead of 68%. The standard deviation still measures the typical distance from the mean.

exam.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: The skewness of the women's earnings is 1.71. Using the chapter's interpretation guideline, how is the distribution's degree of skewness classified?

options.text: Highly skewed
options.feedback: Correct. An absolute skewness above 1 counts as highly skewed under the chapter's guideline.

options.text: Moderately skewed
options.feedback: Revisit the thresholds in the chapter's skewness interpretation guideline (Section 2.1).

options.text: Approximately symmetric
options.feedback: Revisit the thresholds in the chapter's skewness interpretation guideline (Section 2.1).

options.text: Impossible: skewness must lie between −1 and 1
options.feedback: Skewness has no such bound. Revisit the guideline in Section 2.1.

exam.explanation: Guideline: |skewness| < 0.5 approximately symmetric, 0.5–1 moderately skewed, above 1 highly skewed. At 1.71 (positive), earnings are highly right-skewed, with a long tail of high earnings.

exam.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: The chapter reports an excess kurtosis of 4.32 for the women's earnings. What does this indicate?

options.text: The distribution is left-skewed, with a long tail of low earnings.
options.feedback: Direction and asymmetry are what skewness measures. Revisit what kurtosis describes (Key Concepts: Kurtosis).

options.text: The earnings are about 4.32 times as spread out as normal data would be.
options.feedback: Kurtosis does not measure how spread out the data are. Revisit what it describes (Key Concepts: Kurtosis).

options.text: Heavier tails than a normal distribution: extreme earnings are more common.
options.feedback: Correct. Positive excess kurtosis means fatter tails than the normal distribution.

options.text: The typical woman's earnings lie 4.32 standard deviations from the mean.
options.feedback: Kurtosis is a shape measure, not a distance in standard deviations. Revisit Key Concepts: Kurtosis.

exam.explanation: Excess kurtosis compares tail heaviness with the normal distribution (excess kurtosis 0). At 4.32, earnings have much heavier tails: very high earners appear more often than a bell curve would predict.

exam.concept: Shape: skewness and kurtosis (Section 2.1, Key Concepts)
exam.stem: A raw kurtosis of 7.32 corresponds to an excess kurtosis of 4.32.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Excess kurtosis = raw kurtosis − 3, the raw kurtosis of the normal distribution: 7.32 − 3 = 4.32.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how excess kurtosis is defined relative to the normal distribution's raw kurtosis (Section 2.1).

exam.explanation: The normal distribution has a raw kurtosis of 3, so excess kurtosis = raw kurtosis − 3. The chapter's software reports excess kurtosis by default: 7.32 − 3 = 4.32.

exam.stem: Suppose a box plot of a variable shows the median line close to the upper edge of the box and a lower whisker much longer than the upper whisker. What does this suggest about the distribution?

options.text: The distribution is right-skewed.
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter reads skewness from the median's position and the whisker lengths in a box plot (Section 2.1, Box Plot).

options.text: The distribution is left-skewed.
options.feedback: Correct. A long lower whisker and a median pushed toward the top of the box indicate a long tail of low values.

options.text: The distribution is roughly symmetric.
options.feedback: Revisit what a symmetric distribution looks like in a box plot (Section 2.1).

options.text: The median must be equal to the mean.
options.feedback: A box plot does not show the mean. Revisit what the median's position and whisker lengths reveal (Section 2.1).

exam.explanation: In a box plot, a long whisker on one side and a median shifted toward the opposite edge of the box signal skewness toward the long whisker. Here the long tail is on the low side: left skewness (the mirror image of the chapter's earnings box plot).

exam.stem: The chapter's box plot of earnings uses the default whisker rule (1.5 × IQR), with Q1 = $25,000, median = $36,000, and Q3 = $49,000. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The dots beyond the whiskers are data errors that should be deleted.
options.feedback: Revisit what the chapter says the dots beyond the upper whisker represent (Section 2.1, Box Plot).

options.text: The median line sits closer to the lower edge of the box than to the upper edge.
options.feedback: Correct: the median is $11,000 above Q1 but $13,000 below Q3.

options.text: Earnings above $85,000 are drawn as individual outlier dots.
options.feedback: Correct: the upper whisker limit is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = $85,000; the 7 women earning more appear as dots.

options.text: The whiskers always extend to the minimum and maximum values.
options.feedback: Revisit the whisker rule described in Section 2.1.

exam.explanation: The box covers Q1 to Q3, and the median ($36,000) sits closer to Q1 than to Q3, a sign of right skewness. Whiskers reach the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the quartiles: the upper limit is 49,000 + 1.5 × 24,000 = $85,000, and the 7 higher earnings are drawn as outlier dots (real high earners, not errors).

exam.concept: Histograms and kernel density estimates (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2)
exam.stem: The chapter shows two histograms of the same 171 earnings, one with $15,000 bins (Panel A) and one with $7,500 bins (Panel B). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Panel A, with wider bins, shows the secondary peaks more clearly than Panel B.
options.feedback: Revisit what each bin width shows and hides (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2).

options.text: Panel B shows more detail but more noise; Panel A shows the overall shape.
options.feedback: Correct. Bin width trades detail against noise, so it pays to try several widths.

options.text: Panel B is better, because narrower bins remove noise from a histogram.
options.feedback: Revisit what each bin width shows and hides (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2).

options.text: The panels differ, so one of the two histograms must contain an error.
options.feedback: Both panels use the same 171 observations. Revisit what changing the bin width does (Key Concept 2.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.2: the bin width sets the level of detail. The $15,000 bins show the overall right-skewed shape; the $7,500 bins reveal finer structure, such as secondary peaks, at the cost of a noisier look.

exam.concept: Histograms and kernel density estimates (Section 2.2, Key Concept 2.2)
exam.stem: Unlike a histogram, a kernel density estimate does not depend on a choice of bin edges.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A kernel density estimate uses overlapping windows instead of fixed bins, producing a smooth curve.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how a kernel density estimate is built (Section 2.2, Kernel Density Estimate).

exam.explanation: A kernel density estimate is a smoothed histogram without arbitrary bins: it weights nearby observations with overlapping windows. Its smoothness is controlled by a bandwidth rather than by bin edges.

exam.stem: A histogram of the chapter's quarterly U.S. GDP series for 1959 Q1–2020 Q1 shows when the recessions occurred.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what a histogram keeps and what it discards about the order of the observations (Section 2.2).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A histogram groups values into bins and discards their time order; a line chart shows when recessions happened.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.3: line charts display time-ordered data, revealing trends, cycles, and structural breaks such as the 2008–2009 recession. A histogram shows only how often values occur, so the timing of recessions is lost.

exam.concept: Charts for numerical data by category (Section 2.3, Key Concept 2.4)
exam.stem: U.S. health expenditures in 2018 totaled $3,653 billion across 13 categories, of which hospital care was $1,192 billion. What share of total spending went to hospital care?

options.text: About 33%
options.feedback: Correct: 1,192 ÷ 3,653 ≈ 0.326, about a third of all health spending.

options.text: About 48%
options.feedback: Revisit what a share is measured against (Section 2.3).

options.text: About 8%
options.feedback: A share depends on how much is spent in each category, not just on how many categories there are (Section 2.3).

options.text: About 3%
options.feedback: Revisit how a category's share of a total is formed (Section 2.3).

exam.explanation: Share = category ÷ total = 1,192 ÷ 3,653 ≈ 32.6%. Hospital care alone takes about a third of U.S. health spending, more than physician services and drugs combined.

exam.concept: Charts for numerical data by category (Section 2.3, Key Concept 2.4)
exam.stem: Which chart best lets readers compare U.S. health expenditures across the 13 spending categories?

options.text: A bar chart with one bar per category
options.feedback: Correct. Bar length represents each category's value, so comparisons and the ranking are immediate.

options.text: A line chart connecting the 13 categories
options.feedback: Revisit which kinds of data line charts are designed for (Key Concept 2.3).

options.text: A histogram of the 13 expenditure values
options.feedback: A histogram would show how the 13 values are distributed, losing which category is which. Revisit Key Concept 2.4.

options.text: A box plot of the 13 expenditure values
options.feedback: A box plot summarizes a distribution's quartiles and drops the category labels. Revisit Key Concept 2.4.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.4: bar (column) charts display numerical values by category, using bar length so that comparisons are immediate. Sorting the 13 categories by size makes hospital care's dominance obvious.

exam.concept: Charts for categorical data (Section 2.4, Key Concept 2.5)
exam.stem: Of 1,182 recreational fishers, 452 chose a charter boat, 418 a private boat, 178 a pier, and 134 a beach. What is the relative frequency of boat-based fishing (charter or private)?

options.text: About 38%
options.feedback: Revisit how a relative frequency is computed for a group of categories (Section 2.4).

options.text: About 35%
options.feedback: Revisit how a relative frequency is computed for a group of categories (Section 2.4).

options.text: About 50%, because two of the four sites are boats
options.feedback: A relative frequency counts fishers, not sites. Revisit Key Concept 2.5.

options.text: About 74%

exam.explanation: Relative frequency = count ÷ total: (452 + 418) ÷ 1,182 ≈ 73.6% of fishers chose a boat. Charter alone is 38.2% and private boats alone 35.4%.

exam.concept: Charts for categorical data (Section 2.4, Key Concept 2.5)
exam.stem: Which statements about summarizing the fishing-site variable (beach, pier, private boat, charter boat) are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A frequency table of counts and percentages is a natural numerical summary.
options.feedback: Correct: categorical data are summarized by counts and relative frequencies.

options.text: In a pie chart, each slice's area shows that site's share of all fishers.
options.feedback: Correct: slice area corresponds to relative frequency.

options.text: A line chart connecting the four sites is a natural way to display their frequencies.
options.feedback: Revisit which kinds of data line charts are designed for (Key Concept 2.3).

options.text: A bar chart often makes it easier than a pie chart to compare the four sites.
options.feedback: Correct: comparing bar lengths is easier than comparing slice angles.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.5: categorical data are summarized with frequency tables (counts and percentages) and shown with pie charts (slice area = share) or bar charts, which are often easier for comparisons. Line charts suit ordered (time) data, not unordered categories.

exam.stem: After a natural log transformation, the skewness of the women's earnings changes from 1.71 to −0.91. Which description is correct?

options.text: The log made the distribution more skewed, since −0.91 is further from 1.71.
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter's guideline classifies skewness values, and apply it to both numbers (Section 2.1).

options.text: Log earnings are still right-skewed, though less than the original data.
options.feedback: Check this description against the reported skewness of log earnings and the guideline in Section 2.1.

options.text: Log earnings are perfectly symmetric, since logs remove all skewness.
options.feedback: Check the reported skewness of log earnings against the value for a perfectly symmetric distribution.

options.text: Log earnings are much closer to symmetric but moderately left-skewed.
options.feedback: Correct. |−0.91| is well below 1.71; it falls in the moderate range, with a longer tail of low values.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.6: logs compress the long right tail of positive, right-skewed data. Earnings skewness falls from 1.71 (highly right-skewed) to −0.91 (moderately left-skewed), much closer to symmetry.

exam.stem: Log earnings of 10.0 correspond to $22,026 (\( e^{10} \)), and log earnings of 11.0 correspond to $59,874 (\( e^{11} \)). What does a 1-unit increase in log earnings do to earnings?

options.text: It adds about $1 to earnings.
options.feedback: Compare the two dollar amounts in the question. Revisit how log changes translate into dollar changes (Section 2.5).

options.text: It raises earnings by about 100%.
options.feedback: The 'change in log ≈ proportional change' rule only works for small changes. Compare the two dollar amounts in the question.

options.text: It multiplies earnings by about 2.72.
options.feedback: Correct: 59,874 ÷ 22,026 ≈ 2.718 = e. Each 1-unit rise in the log multiplies earnings by e.

options.text: It adds about $37,848 at every earnings level.
options.feedback: Revisit whether a change in logs corresponds to a fixed dollar amount or to a proportional change (Section 2.5).

exam.explanation: A 1-unit increase in ln(earnings) multiplies earnings by \( e \approx 2.718 \), a 172% increase: \( e^{11}/e^{10} = e \). Only small log changes are approximately percentage changes (0.05 ≈ 5%).

exam.stem: Suppose a variable records each firm's annual profit, including losses (negative values). Taking its natural log directly is a sound way to reduce its skewness.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's list of when NOT to use a log transformation (Section 2.5).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The natural log is undefined for zero and negative values, so profits with losses cannot be logged directly.

exam.explanation: Section 2.5 'When NOT to use log transformation': the log is undefined for zero and negative values. Logs suit strictly positive, right-skewed variables such as earnings, prices, and GDP.

exam.stem: Mean earnings are $41,413 and the standard deviation is $25,527. The highest earner in the sample makes $172,000. What is her z-score, approximately?

options.text: About 5.1
options.feedback: Correct: (172,000 − 41,413) ÷ 25,527 ≈ 5.1 standard deviations above the mean, an extreme value.

options.text: About 3.2
options.feedback: Revisit the z-score formula and check each quantity you used (Section 2.5).

options.text: About 5.3
options.feedback: Revisit the z-score formula and check each quantity you used (Section 2.5).

options.text: About 6.7
options.feedback: Revisit the z-score formula and check each quantity you used (Section 2.5).

exam.explanation: \( z = (x - \bar{x})/s = (172{,}000 - 41{,}413)/25{,}527 \approx 5.1 \). She earns about five standard deviations above the mean, far beyond the |z| > 3 'very unusual' mark.

exam.stem: Why do economists standardize variables into z-scores?

options.text: To adjust values measured over time for inflation
options.feedback: Revisit what a z-score expresses and what it is used for (Section 2.5).

options.text: To make every observation a positive number
options.feedback: Revisit what the sign of a z-score tells you (Section 2.5).

options.text: To convert every observation into a percentage
options.feedback: Revisit the units in which a z-score is expressed (Key Concepts: Z-Score).

options.text: To compare variables measured in different units
options.feedback: Correct. A z-score expresses each observation in standard deviations from its mean, so variables in dollars, minutes, or degrees become comparable.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.6: z-scores standardize data to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, expressing each observation as standard deviations above or below the mean, so variables measured in different units can be compared. Standardizing does not change a distribution's shape.

exam.stem: Suppose a news report says U.S. monthly home sales rose sharply from February to June. Before concluding that the housing market is recovering, what should you check first?

options.text: Whether the figures are in real or nominal dollars
options.feedback: Even if sales were measured in dollars, prices change too little over four months to produce a sharp rise. Revisit Key Concept 2.7.

options.text: Whether the figures are seasonally adjusted
options.feedback: Correct. Raw home sales rise every spring and summer; only seasonally adjusted figures show whether the rise is unusual.

options.text: Whether a histogram of monthly sales is right-skewed
options.feedback: The shape of the distribution of all monthly sales says nothing about why sales changed between two particular months. Revisit Section 2.6.

options.text: Whether the median of monthly sales exceeds the mean
options.feedback: Comparing the mean and the median describes the distribution as a whole, not a change between two particular months. Revisit Section 2.6.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 2.7 and Section 2.6: home sales have strong seasonality (peaks in late spring and summer, troughs in January–February). A February-to-June rise is normal; seasonally adjusted data reveal whether the market is really recovering.

exam.stem: An analyst wants to compare U.S. living standards in 1960 and 2020 using GDP. Which adjustments to the GDP series are needed? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Converting nominal GDP into real GDP (constant dollars)
options.feedback: Correct: real values remove the effect of inflation.

options.text: Converting the GDP series into z-scores
options.feedback: Revisit which adjustments Section 2.6 lists for comparing values over time.

options.text: Taking an 11-month moving average of the series
options.feedback: Revisit what problem a moving average addresses (Section 2.6).

options.text: Dividing GDP by the population (per capita)
options.feedback: Correct: per capita values adjust for population growth.

exam.explanation: Section 2.6 and Key Concept 2.7: real values adjust for inflation and per capita values for population size. Comparing living standards across decades uses real GDP per capita, which rose from about $17,700 in early 1959 to about $57,600 in early 2020 (the first quarter, the series' last observation), in 2012 dollars.
